extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners researching U.S. free-speech law (law students, journalists, policymakers, advocates)
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of the categories of speech that are excluded from First Amendment protection in the United States, and the legal tests, precedents, statutes, and doctrines that define those exceptions. Covers case law, statutory rules, and institutional practice across schools, workplaces, national security, and online platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may impose a prior restraint only if it can show that punishment after the fact is not a sufficient remedy and that allowing the speech would "surely result in direct, immediate, and irreparable damage to our Nation and its people" (New York Times Co. v. United States). U.S. courts have not permitted most prior restraints since Near v. Minnesota (1931).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High bar for pre-publication censorship; prior restraint is generally disfavored. Historical exceptions and limited contexts may exist (see Near, New York Times Co. v. United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: School-sponsored publication prior-restraint exception (Hazelwood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier allowed censorship by a school of content in a school-sponsored student newspaper on the basis that the paper was sponsored by the school and subject to rules about inappropriate articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a student publication is school-sponsored and not established as a public forum for student expression, schools may impose content-based restrictions consistent with Hazelwood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsehoods — limited criminal exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws against commercial fraud, counterfeit currency, and perjury have been upheld; however, false statements of fact are generally protected speech (United States v. Alvarez held the government had not demonstrated that false statements generally should constitute a new category of unprotected speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False statements are not categorically unprotected; only narrow, well-defined falsehood-related offenses (fraud, perjury, counterfeiting) are routinely upheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incitement to imminent lawless action (Brandenburg test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that incites imminent lawless action is unprotected under the Brandenburg test (replacing the older 'clear and present danger' test from Schenck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard requires intent, imminence, and likelihood of producing lawless action; mere advocacy of violence in the abstract is usually protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting words
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflammatory words that are either injurious by themselves or might cause the hearer to immediately retaliate or breach the peace; such 'fighting words' are not necessarily protected under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fighting-words doctrine is narrowly applied; context and immediacy are crucial to determine whether words fall into this unprotected category.

rubrics_metrics.name: True threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that constitute 'true threats' are not protected (see Watts v. United States, Virginia v. Black).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts analyze whether a reasonable person would interpret the statement as a serious expression of intent to harm; political hyperbole is often distinguished from true threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity — Miller test
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscenity is unprotected speech defined by the Miller test: the material (1) appeals to prurient interest, (2) depicts or describes sexual conduct in a patently offensive way according to contemporary community standards, and (3) lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied primarily to hard-core pornography; community standards and the three-part analysis are essential. Statutory and enforcement contours vary by medium and jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child pornography
rubrics_metrics.description: Child pornography is categorically unprotected (see New York v. Ferber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict prohibitions apply to production, distribution, and possession; constitutional exceptions that protect adult-oriented obscenity do not extend to child pornography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation (libel and slander) and actual malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on libel and slander can give rise to civil liability; New York Times Co. v. Sullivan established the 'actual malice' standard for public-figure plaintiffs, raising the bar to recover for defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private-figure plaintiffs face a lower standard in many contexts. Defamation doctrines balance reputational interests against robust public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements in federal matters as crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Making false statements in 'matters within the jurisdiction' of the federal government is a criminal offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory crime distinct from civil defamation doctrine; scope depends on the statute and factual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invasion of privacy torts
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil liability can attach for invasion of privacy (see Time, Inc. v. Hill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy torts interact with First Amendment concerns; courts balance privacy interests against newsworthiness and public-interest speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional infliction of emotional distress
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme or outrageous speech can give rise to tort liability for intentional infliction of emotional distress (see Hustler Magazine v. Falwell, Texas v. Johnson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-figure status and related First Amendment protections can limit recovery; context and degree of outrageousness are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign contributions (Buckley) and independent expenditures (Citizens United / SpeechNow.org)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaign contributions and independent political expenditures are regulated under First Amendment doctrine: Buckley v. Valeo addresses contributions; Citizens United and SpeechNow.org address independent expenditures and corporate/political speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different rules apply to direct contributions to candidates versus independent expenditures; corporate and association speech received renewed protection in Citizens United.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government speech doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may censor or control speech when the speech is its own (the 'government speech' doctrine), producing contentious decisions over the doctrine's breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If speech is classified as government speech, First Amendment constraints on the government are reduced or altered; courts examine authorship, funding, and governmental control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-employee speech (Garcetti / Pickering / Lane)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by public employees pursuant to their official duties are not protected by the First Amendment from employer discipline (Garcetti). Speech by public employees speaking as citizens on matters of public concern can be protected (Pickering; Lane v. Franks clarifies application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the speech was made pursuant to official duties, whether it addresses a matter of public concern, and whether balancing tests (government employer interests vs. employee speech interests) favor protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony & citizen speech edge cases (Lane v. Burrows summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who testifies in court and where that testimony is not part of their employment duties testifies as a citizen and has First Amendment protection; speech that is an actual part of job duties may not be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases distinguish speech that is merely related to duties from speech that is integral to job responsibilities; whistleblower and retaliation concerns are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student speech doctrines (Tinker, Bethel, Hazelwood, Morse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tinker: broad protection for student speech unless there is 'substantial interference with school discipline or the rights of others.' Bethel: schools can discipline indecent but non-obscene student speech. Hazelwood: schools can censor school-sponsored publications not established as public forums. Morse: suspension supported for banner 'BONG HiTS 4 JESUS' at a school-supervised event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the appropriate precedent by context: general student speech (Tinker), school-sponsored/activity speech (Hazelwood, Morse), lewd/indecent speech (Bethel). Court holdings vary by facts and forum status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness / overbreadth in school policies (Lowry v. Watson Chapel example)
rubrics_metrics.description: School policies (dress codes, literature distribution) that are vague or unnecessarily prohibitive of criticism can be struck down (Lowry v. Watson Chapel School District).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies regulating student expression must be clear and narrowly tailored to avoid chilling protected speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: National security / military secrets restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing, gathering, or collecting national security information (military secrets) is not protected speech in the U.S.; certain national-defense-related information is automatically classified or restricted (e.g., Atomic Energy Act for nuclear data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized creation, publication, sale, or transfer of designated defense information, Restricted Data, or classified materials can be criminally prohibited; context, intent, and classification status matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and deterrents for national-security disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond criminal penalties, the government may use employment contracts, loss of government employment, monetary penalties, non-disclosure agreements, forfeiture of property, injunctions, revocation of passports, and prior restraint to deter sensitive disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mix of criminal and administrative remedies is used to prevent and punish unauthorized disclosures involving national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy regarding inventions (Invention Secrecy Act / Voluntary Tender Act history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes such as the Voluntary Tender Act and the Invention Secrecy Act authorize withholding certification of inventions and preventing inventors from publishing or sharing information about inventions that might harm national security, with attached criminal penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government secrecy orders can require inventors to limit dissemination; statutory frameworks and penalties apply where national-security interests are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic classification of nuclear information (Atomic Energy Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atomic Energy Act of 1954 automatically classifies data concerning (1) design, manufacture, or utilization of atomic weapons; (2) the production of special nuclear material; or (3) the use of special nuclear material in the production of energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure or unauthorized handling of such data is tightly controlled and may be criminalized regardless of intent to harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on teaching/distributing weapons-making information (18 U.S.C. § 842(p))
rubrics_metrics.description: 18 U.S.C. § 842(p) makes it an offense to 'teach or demonstrate the making or use of an explosive, a destructive device, or a weapon of mass destruction, or to distribute by any means information pertaining to, in whole or in part, the manufacture or use of' such devices, when intending or knowing the information will be used to further a federal crime of violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This federal statute supplements other laws preventing dissemination of bombmaking and related information for criminal purposes; constitutionality in some contexts remains litigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast obscenity/regulation by FCC
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Communications Commission censors over-the-air television and radio for obscenity and related content (Roth v. United States contexts), but does not have the same regulatory power over cable, satellite television, or satellite radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory authority varies by transmission medium; broadcasters face stricter content regulation than many other platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet speech protections and limits (Reno, COPA, CIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reno v. ACLU extended full First Amendment protection to the Internet, striking down portions of the Communications Decency Act; later congressional attempts such as COPA have been invalidated. United States v. American Library Association upheld Congress's authority to require content-control software as a condition of certain federal funding (Children's Internet Protection Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet speech generally enjoys strong protection, but funding conditions, time/place/manner restrictions, and child-protection measures can create limited constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private actors and private property limits on speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment restricts government action, not private actors; incorporation via Gitlow applies speech protections against state actors. Whether private landowners may exclude speech (e.g., shopping centers) is vigorously litigated (Lloyd Corp. v. Tanner; Pruneyard Shopping Center v. Robins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permission and forum status (private property vs. designated public forum) control speech rights in private spaces; state constitutions can provide additional protections (Pruneyard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media platforms' policy autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Privately owned social media platforms (Facebook, Twitter, etc.) are not bound by the First Amendment, though they sometimes ban or censor users at government requests and adopt moderation standards informed by court concepts like the public-figure doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform governance is primarily contractual and policy-driven; designers often borrow legal tests but are not legally compelled by the First Amendment except in specific state-created-forum scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: College campus free-speech policy standards and disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Public colleges and universities are constrained by the First Amendment, limiting the ability to impose speech codes; institutional statements like the 'Chicago Statement' advocate minimal censorship, while organizations like FIRE publish comparative assessments and rankings of campus speech policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campus speech governance involves balancing academic freedom, administrative policies, and civil-liberties advocacy; marketplace-of-ideas rationales and forum analyses inform policy development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections for private-sector employees' off-duty speech (state statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states provide statutory protections for employees' lawful off-duty speech and activities: Connecticut (statutory protection unless activity substantially interferes with job duties), New York (Section 201-d protects off-duty political/recreational activities with some exceptions for conflicts of interest), Colorado (lawful off-duty-conduct statute with exception for activities reasonably related to employment), California (Labor Code §96(k) and §98.6(a) broadly restrict adverse actions for lawful off-duty conduct, with limited exceptions for illegal activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State laws vary considerably: some provide broad protection for off-duty expression while others permit employer action when speech materially interferes with job duties, involves proprietary interests, or constitutes illegal conduct (e.g., participation in the 2021 Capitol riots).
